source.title: Subspace Rerouting: Using Mechanistic Interpretability to Craft Adversarial Attacks against Large Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The post reports an input-optimization attack that targets activations with negative cosine similarity to the refusal direction and says the resulting suffixes jailbreak the model. This tests whether an attack can suppress the direction through a different intervention from the original ablation method.
record.gate_note: The post also reports attacks targeting probe-defined subspaces and attention patterns, but these do not establish that the refusal direction is what those attacks suppress. Figures for cosine similarities and KL divergence are described but their plotted numerical values are not present in the text. Values used to select targets or tune the method are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The post builds an input-suffix attack (SSR) whose loss pushes activations to negative cosine similarity with the difference-in-means refusal direction. It reports that the resulting suffixes jailbreak Llama 3.2 1b while keeping the direction suppressed across layers. This bears on V3 by a different method from the original. The attack is designed to suppress the direction, so it shows that input-level suppression suffices. It does not show that other jailbreaks work this way.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct, with two additions. SSR converts runtime interventions such as refusal-direction steering into input suffixes that jailbreak small models (>80% on four models). SSR matches the effect of steering without intervening at inference, and runtime-steered activations revert in later layers. The author also notes limited experiments, a 3B-parameter ceiling, and possible failure on larger models.
record.recipe_differences: Uses gradient-based input optimization to reroute activations toward a target subspace, including negative cosine similarity to the refusal direction; it does not project the direction out of the residual stream or add it as in the original intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported setup varies target layers and steering coefficient; SSR uses layers 5, 8, 10, and 14 with coefficient -3, while the runtime-steering comparison uses coefficient -2. The post also reports model-dependent results for attention-head targeting.

fits_no_version.finding: Runtime steering against the refusal direction (coefficient -2) produces activations whose cosine similarity reverts toward the harmful pattern in later layers. SSR inputs do not revert. KL divergence is said to partly support the view that steered activations are off-distribution.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Runtime steering against the refusal direction yields off-distribution activations that later layers partly undo, while input-level suppression persists.

fits_no_version.finding: SSR jailbreak success is reported at >80% on four small models, but not attributed to refusal-direction targeting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subspace-targeted input optimization achieves high jailbreak rates on small chat models.

fits_no_version.finding: Rerouting activations within a probe-defined subspace is described as enough to jailbreak Llama 3.2 1b.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input perturbations that move activations from probe-defined harmful to harmless subspaces can jailbreak models.

fits_no_version.finding: Attention-head-targeted attacks have nonzero success on every model. On Llama 3.2 3B and Gemma 2 2b they work only when the targeted head is a safety head.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Rerouting attention in safety heads can produce jailbreaks.

fits_no_version.finding: A 'reverse logit lens' that optimizes input tokens toward the layer-10 refusal direction in Llama 3.2 1b yields harmful words (e.g. bomb-related, slurs). No rate is given beyond about one good run in three.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input tokens that most activate the refusal direction are harmful-content words.

record.problems: The author says experiments were not extensive and notes a personal-computer limit, with work stopped at 3B parameters. Numerical success rates, sample sizes, and uncertainty estimates are not given in the post. Some reported activation and KL results are only described from figures whose values are absent in the supplied text. The author notes that Gemma 2 2b often redirects the attack into a harmless conversation.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for normal and random-suffix cosine conditions or KL-divergence comparisons because the supplied text does not state their outcomes numerically or with a sufficiently specific result for each condition. No row for the reported baseline being only slightly worse is included because it compares the post's new method rather than measuring the refusal-direction intervention itself.

untested.parts: Untested: whether existing or natural jailbreaks work by suppressing the direction (only a direction-targeted attack is shown). Also untested: whether training against ablation adds robustness. No success rate is reported for the direction-targeted attack.
No directional ablation, no addition to induce refusal, and no capability evaluation.

missing.what: Cosine-similarity curves for the Normal and Random-suffix runs, and the KL-divergence comparison. These are the baselines for r2, and their values are given only in the figure.
missing.locator: Section 'Introducing Subspace Rerouting', cosine-similarity and KL figures

missing.what: Per-model success rates for refusal-direction-targeted SSR, referred to in the arXiv paper (2503.06269) but not in the post.

record.verdict_notes: This is a LessWrong post summarizing arXiv:2503.06269. Results are described qualitatively, largely from figures, without rates or sample sizes. The V3 support is weak: the attack is designed to suppress the direction, which shows that suppression suffices but not that jailbreaks in general rely on it.

versions.untested_parts: No ablation of the difference-in-means direction across layers and positions, no addition of that direction to induce refusals, and no general-capability evaluation.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is reported.
The post reports input attacks targeting the refusal direction, but does not test training against ablation or whether such training adds robustness.
The post discusses probes and attention heads as other attack targets but does not test whether refusal itself requires an affine, conic, or multi-direction description.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision is tested.
No transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models is tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or timing is reported.

tranche.reason: A different method (input-suffix optimisation toward negative cosine with the diff-in-means direction) bears on whether suppressing the direction jailbreaks. Borderline T4, since the evidence is mostly the attack's own success, but it also reports how direction similarity evolves across layers versus runtime steering.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] id for the single V3 verdict, so l1 was assigned by position. The author admits an unmatched comparison: coefficient -3 for SSR vs -2 for runtime steering. Quantitative ASRs belong to the companion arXiv:2503.06269 record, not this post.

statements.correction: This post (LessWrong, informal) gives no ASR for refusal-direction SSR. r1/r2: Llama 3.2 1b; SSR suffixes of length 5, target layers 5, 8, 10, 14, coefficient -3. Successful suffixes are said to jailbreak and to keep negative cosine similarity to the refusal direction across layers. Runtime steering (coefficient -2) reverts in later layers. Only general claim: SSR >80% success on Qwen 2.5 1.5b, Llama 3.2 1b/3b and Gemma 2 2b, cited from the paper, no variant named.
statements.problem: The statement cites r1 and r2 from this post but gives Steering-SSR numbers (Qwen2.5 1.5b ASR 0.12 to 0.95) that are not in the post. The post's rows are Llama 3.2 1b and qualitative. The 'preprint with controls on four models' description fits arXiv:2503.06269, not this LessWrong post.
